title: Tested teachings
hookLine: four ways that undo the holy life and four that give no comfort

lines: A LOUD EVENING BY A POOL.
cards: Evening, by a pool near the city of Kosambī. A wanderer named Sandaka is sitting with a big group of his students, and they're loud, talking about kings and armies and food and gossip, the way any group talks.
Then he sees Ānanda walking toward them and hushes everyone. Quiet, he says, here comes one of the Buddha's monks; they like quiet. Sandaka invites him to say something about his teacher's way.
And Ānanda, rather than praising it, starts with how to tell when a way of life isn't worth following.

teach.h: FOUR WAYS THAT UNDO THE TRAINING.
teach.b: Ānanda describes eight cases. Four, he says, undo the holy life completely.
They're teachings that say, in different ways, that what you do makes no difference: no fruit from good or bad action, no cause for purity, everything fixed in advance.

If that's the teaching, a sensible person reasons: then why train at all? The text names views held by some teachers of that time; this lesson keeps to the shape of the argument. The next four aren't wrong exactly.

teach.h: THE ALL-KNOWING TEACHER, BITTEN BY A DOG.
teach.b: First, a teacher who claims to know and see everything, always. Yet he walks into an empty house and gets no food, gets bitten by a dog, meets a wild elephant, and has to ask people's names and the way to the village.
Second, a teacher who relies only on tradition: some of it well remembered, some not; some true, some not.
Third, a teacher who relies only on reasoning: some well reasoned, some badly. Fourth, a teacher who is simply confused, and when asked a question wriggles like an eel.
In each case, Ānanda says, a wise person notices, and quietly looks elsewhere. And he doesn't say, trust us instead.
He describes a training a person can check for themselves: conduct, then calm, then understanding, each with results that can be seen.
The same caution shows up elsewhere in the Pali texts: a teaching isn't settled by authority, tradition or cleverness alone. Look at what it does in a life.

how: Buddhist teachers in several traditions encourage students to test teachings in their own experience rather than accept them on authority alone, sometimes citing this sutta alongside the Kālāma Sutta.

o: lessons passed down unchanged by tradition
ways of life you can check by their results
teachings approved by a council of elders

games.q: four that give no comfort: tap the pairs.

s: in this sutta Ānanda says tradition is always wrong
he says it's uncertain: some is well remembered and true, some isn't.
Sandaka hushes his students when he sees Ānanda coming
he tells them the Buddha's monks like quiet.
the sutta asks people to trust the Buddha's monks instead
Ānanda describes a way whose results a person can test for themselves.

games.q: a teacher claims to know everything, always. then he walks into an empty house and has to ask the way to the village. in Ānanda's account, what does a wise person do?
o: notice the gap, and look elsewhere
games.why: Ānanda calls this a holy life without comfort: the claim doesn't match the life, so a wise person quietly looks elsewhere.

practice: Choose one idea you've been living by, from a book, a parent, a podcast, even from this path, and ask slowly: do I hold it only because it was handed to me, or only because it sounds clever?
Then ask what it has actually done in your life, and in the lives of people who follow it, and let the answer be honest.

wordCard.voice: Tested teachings. Ānanda's eight cases: four teachings that undo the holy life, and four that give no comfort, from claimed omniscience to eel-wriggling.

orig.note: Pali anussava: what is heard and handed down, oral tradition. one of the four uncertain grounds.

carryVoice: Your line: test the teaching. Even a teacher who claims to know everything may have to ask the way. That's day four hundred sixty-six.
